etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English hitten (“to hit, strike, make contact with”), from Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”), from Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew”).

Cognate with Icelandic hitta (“to meet”), Danish hitte (“to find”), Latin caedō (“to kill”), Albanian qit (“to hit, throw, pull out, release”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To administer a blow to, directly or with a weapon or missile.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter II, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Orion hit a rabbit once; but though sore wounded it got to the bury, and, struggling in, the arrow caught the side of the hole and was drawn out. Indeed, a nail filed sharp is not of much avail as an arrowhead; you must have it barbed, and that was a little beyond our skill.

quote.citation: 1922-1927, Frank Harris, My Life and Loves:
quote.text: He tried to hit me but I dodged the blow and went out to plot revenge.

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[[Episode 15]]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Bello: (Shouts) Good, by the rumping jumping general! That's the best bit of news I heard these six weeks. Here, don't keep me waiting, damn you! (He slaps her face)Bello: (Whimpers) You're after hitting me. I'll tell […]

quote.citation: 1934, Robert E. Howard, The Slugger's Game:
quote.text: I hunted him for half a hour, aiming to learn him to hit a man with a table-leg and then run, but I didn't find him.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To come into contact with forcefully and suddenly.

quote.citation: 1726 October 28, [Jonathan Swift], Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.  […]  [Gulliver’s Travels], volume I, London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, part II (A Voyage to Brobdingnag):
quote.text: a dozen apples, each of them near as large as a Bristol barrel, came tumbling about my ears; one of them hit me on the back as I chanced to stoop, and knocked me down flat on my face.

quote.citation: 1882, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Doctor Grimshawe's Secret: A romance:
quote.text: Meanwhile the street boys kept up a shower of mud balls, many of which hit the Doctor, while the rest were distributed upon his assailants.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To strike against something.

quote.citation: a. 1705, John Locke, “An Examination of P[ère] Malebranche’s Opinion of Seeing All Things in God”, in Posthumous Works of Mr. John Locke: […], London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], published 1706, →OCLC:
quote.text: If bodies be extension alone,  […] how can they move and hit one against another?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To activate a button or key by pressing and releasing it.
(transitive, slang) To kill a person, usually on the instructions of a third party.

quote.citation: 1973, Mario Puzo, Francis Ford Coppola, The Godfather Part II (screenplay, second draft)
quote.text: FREDO: Mikey, why would they ever hit poor old Frankie Five-Angels? I loved that ole sonuvabitch.

definitions.definition: (transitive, military) To attack, especially amphibiously.
(figurative, transitive, intransitive) To affect someone, as if dealing a blow to that person.
(heading, physical) To strike.
(transitive) To manage to touch (a target) in the right place.
(transitive, colloquial) To switch on.
(transitive, music, informal) To commence playing.
(transitive, colloquial) To briefly visit.
(transitive, informal) To encounter an obstacle or other difficulty.
(transitive, informal) To reach or achieve.

quote.citation: 2012 August 1, Owen Gibson, “London 2012: rowers Glover and Stanning win Team GB's first gold medal”, in Guardian Unlimited‎[1]:
quote.text: And her success with Glover, a product of the National Lottery-funded Sporting Giants talent identification programme, will also spark relief among British officials who were starting to fret a little about hitting their target of equalling fourth in the medal table from Beijing.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To meet or reach what was aimed at or desired; to succeed, often by luck.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: And oft it hits / Where hope is coldest and despair most fits.

quote.citation: 1733, [Jonathan Swift], On Poetry: A Rapsody, Dublin, London:  […]  [R. Fleming] [a]nd sold by J. Huggonson, […], →OCLC, page 3, lines 1–2:
quote.text: All Human Race wou’d fain be Wits, / And Millions miſs, for one that hits.

definitions.definition: To guess; to light upon or discover.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Thou hast hit it.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XLVI, page 69:
quote.text: And we shall sit at endless feast,⁠Enjoying each the other’s good;⁠What vaster dream can hit the moodOf Love on earth?

definitions.definition: (heading) To attain, to achieve.
(transitive) To affect negatively.
(figuratively) To attack.

quote.citation: 2016 March 3, Nick Gass, quoting Donald Trump, “Trump on small hands: 'I guarantee you there's no problem'”, in Politico‎[2]:
quote.text: I have to say this, he hit my hands. Nobody has ever hit my hands. I’ve never heard of this one. Look at those hands. Are they small hands?

definitions.definition: (transitive, card games) In blackjack, to deal a card to.
(intransitive, baseball) To come up to bat.
(backgammon) To take up, or replace by a piece belonging to the opposing player; said of a single unprotected piece on a point.
(heading, games) To make a play.
(transitive, computing, programming) To use; to connect to.
(transitive, US, slang) To have sex with.
(transitive, US, slang) To inhale an amount of smoke from a narcotic substance, particularly marijuana.

quote.citation: 2005, “Stay Fly”, in Jordan Houston, Darnell Carlton, Paul Beauregard, Premro Smith, Marlon Goodwin, David Brown, Willie Hutchinson (lyrics), Most Known Unknown‎[3], performed by Three 6 Mafia (featuring Young Buck, 8 Ball, and MJG), Sony BMG:
quote.text: Tastes like fruit when you hit it; got to have bread to get it.

definitions.definition: (transitive, bodybuilding) (of an exercise) to affect, to work a body part.
(transitive, bodybuilding) to work out
A blow; a punch; a striking against; the collision of one body against another; the stroke that touches anything.

Translated into English Verse.  […]  Together with the Satires of Aulus Persius Flaccus. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: So he the fam'd Cilician fencer prais'd, / And, at each hit, with wonder seem'd amaz'd.

definitions.definition: Something very successful, such as a song, film, or video game, that receives widespread recognition and acclaim.

quote.citation: 1848, “Her Majesty's Theatre”, in The Musical World‎[4], volume 23:
quote.text: Marie Taglioni was another hit for Her Majesty's Theatre last season, and will be a hit again this season […]

quote.citation: 2012 February 9, Tasha Robinson, “Film: Review: Chico & Rita”, in (Please provide the book title or journal name)‎[5]:
quote.text: Chico & Rita opens in the modern era, as an aged, weary Chico shines shoes in his native Cuba. Then a song heard on the radio—a hit he wrote and recorded with Rita in their youth—carries him back to 1948 Havana, where they first met.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A blow; a calamitous or damaging occurrence.
An attack on a location, person or people.
In the game of Battleship, a correct guess at where one's opponent ship is.
A collision of a projectile with the target.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Benedict le Vay, “The heroes of Soham...”, in RAIL, number 948, page 43:
quote.text: But signalman Bridges was never to answer driver Gimbert's desperate question. A deafening, massive blast blew the wagon to shreds, the 44 high-explosive bombs exploding like simultaneous hits from the aircraft they should have been dropped from. The station was instantly reduced to bits of debris, and the line to a huge crater.

definitions.definition: (computing, Internet) A match found by searching a computer system or search engine
(Internet) A measured visit to a web site, a request for a single file from a web server.
An approximately correct answer in a test set.
(baseball) The complete play, when the batter reaches base without the benefit of a walk, error, or fielder’s choice.
(colloquial) A dose of an illegal or addictive drug.
A premeditated murder done for criminal or political purposes.

quote.citation: 2023 August 30, Megan K. Stack, Rob Stothard, “He Was Shot 14 Times at the Dinner Table. His Children Want to Know if Britain Ordered the Hit.”, in The New York Times‎[6], →ISSN:
quote.text: The questions that have always haunted the family — who ordered the hit, and why, and who in London might have known — remain unanswered.

definitions.definition: (dated) A peculiarly apt expression or turn of thought; a phrase which hits the mark.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], (please specify |epistle=I to IV), London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: What late he called a blessing, now was wit, / And God's good providence, a lucky hit.

definitions.definition: (backgammon) A move that throws one of the opponent's men back to the entering point.
(backgammon) A game won after the adversary has removed some of his men. It counts for less than a gammon.
Very successful.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hit (“it”), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this, here”). Cognate with Dutch het (“it”). More at it; also note 'it.

definitions.definition: (dialectal) It.

quote.citation: 1922, Philip Gengembre Hubert, The Atlantic monthly, volume 130:
quote.text: But how hit was to come about didn't appear.

quote.citation: 1998, Nancy A. Walker, What's so funny?: humor in American culture:
quote.text: Now, George, grease it good, an' let hit slide down the hill hits own way.
